<description>
{
 "summary": "Hardens the read-only Berkeley DB parser used during wallet migration and `bitcoin-wallet` execution against crafted database files. It tracks visited B-tree and overflow pages across tree traversal to prevent duplicate page visits, loops, or shared chains. It also bounds the cumulative size of records on internal and data pages to the page size, and ensures overflow page payload lengths do not exceed page boundaries.",
 "problem": "Crafted BDB files supplied to `migratewallet` or `bitcoin-wallet` can trigger infinite loops, exponential traversal time, or massive memory inflation. A B-tree page referenced by multiple parent nodes is repeatedly traversed, cycles of empty overflow pages loop indefinitely, and duplicated record index entries or oversized overflow offsets can expand small files into hundreds of megabytes of allocated memory.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'On master an ~8 KB file built this way doesn't finish.'",
  "PR description: 'A single 64 KB page can turn into ~500 MB this way. On master a 256 KB file took migratewallet from 54 MB to ~800 MB.'",
  "Commit f7e0d7e24b: '34959 added two errors for invalid overflow records, but did not add them to the errors the wallet_bdb_parser target expects, so the target aborts on inputs that reach them.'"
 ],

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
